clue.text: Most agree to differ about beginning to scrap large tanks

indicators.note: letters made to differ from their printed order are being rearranged
one thing placed about another wraps round it, so the shuffled letters go round the kept one

parts.note: the two words' letters rearranged

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Most people consent to differ over whether to start scrapping some big tanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Gasometers are the huge cylindrical gas-holders once common in British towns, literally large storage tanks.

clue.text: Sea-marker buoys in Greek port

indicators.note: things put in something else sit inside it, so the buoys go within the abbreviation

explanation.surface: Buoys marking the sea lanes in a harbour in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek port' reads as one phrase, but Greek is only the GK wrapper; the port is in Poland.
explanation.definitionFit: Gdansk is a major Baltic seaport city in northern Poland.

clue.text: Fuss about most of extraordinary bottles of carbonated drink?

indicators.note: something that bottles another holds it inside, as a bottle holds liquid

parts.note: ado is fuss or bother

explanation.surface: A row over the remarkable number of fizzy-drink bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: SICK loses its K, and the reversed fuss sits inside what remains. The question mark admits the adjective is a rare coinage.
explanation.definitionFit: Sodaic is a rare adjective meaning pertaining to or containing soda, so it describes a carbonated drink.

clue.text: French teacher promoted German wine around Italy

parts.note: as in 'made captain', raised to a rank

indicators.note: the wine wraps around the country's abbreviation, holding it inside

parts.note: a white wine from the Mosel valley in Germany
international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A French teacher gets promoted and celebrates with German wine in Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: In British schools and households a mademoiselle was the title for a French governess or teacher of French.

clue.text: Fold stuff

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a flat pleat sewn into fabric
second meaning: British slang for food, especially snacks

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as two verbs for packing things away; the second is the noun for food.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuck is a pleat in cloth, and in British slang tuck is food or sweets, eaten as stuff.

clue.text: Fell over after a couple of drinks, second one up in US recreation area

parts.note: the first of the two drinks, a spirit

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: the second drink, a sip or mouthful

indicators.note: knocked over means turned upside down, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: a fell is a hill or moorland in northern England

explanation.surface: Someone fell over after two drinks in an American games room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fell' looks like a verb but is the noun for upland moor. The two drinks are RUM and SUP; only the second turns up.
explanation.definitionFit: A rumpus room is the American term for a basement or den kept for play and recreation.

clue.text: Walk to/from back

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so these letters are read in reverse

parts.note: taken as written
'of' can mean from, as in 'of noble birth'

explanation.surface: A note that the walk goes there and back.
explanation.walkthrough: The slash just joins the two little words; together they read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To foot it is an idiom for travelling on foot, so to foot means to walk.

clue.text: Schiller's work, note, raised in every other piece of old melody

indicators.note: placed in the other letters, so it sits inside them
taking every other piece means keeping alternate letters, starting with the first

parts.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising a word lifts it bottom to top, so it reads backwards

parts.note: a jot is a brief note, as in jot down

explanation.surface: Describing Schiller's poem as built from an old tune with a note added.
explanation.definitionFit: Ode to Joy is Friedrich Schiller's 1785 poem, later set by Beethoven in his Ninth Symphony.

clue.text: Crawling cat bites poor Daisy …

indicators.note: something in poor shape is out of order, so its letters are rearranged
whatever bites something holds it between its jaws, so the cat goes round it

parts.note: a tom is a male cat
the name's letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A creeping cat sinks its teeth into poor Daisy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crawling' looks like the cat's movement, but it means fawning; the ellipsis runs the idea on into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Crawling in the sense of grovelling servility is exactly toadyism, the behaviour of a toady or flatterer.

clue.text: Base impeded AAC officer

indicators.note: something base is debased or corrupted, so these letters are degraded into a new order

parts.note: all ten letters rearranged

explanation.surface: An army base hampered an officer of the Army Air Corps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' reads as a military base, but it is the anagram signal; AAC is the British Army Air Corps.
explanation.definitionFit: An aide-de-camp is a military officer serving as personal assistant to a senior commander.

clue.text: Cycling permitted in Cuban tobacco field

indicators.note: letters cycling round move from the front to the back in order

parts.note: gave can mean allowed, as in 'gave him leave'

explanation.surface: Cycling is allowed through Cuba's tobacco plantations.
explanation.walkthrough: The first two letters of the verb move round to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Vega is the Spanish word, used in Cuba, for a fertile tract where tobacco is grown.

clue.text: … displaying which, Cynthia shops around

indicators.note: letters moved around are put into a different order

parts.note: all twelve letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: Cynthia shops around showing that grovelling streak.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 8 Down: 'which' stands for toadyism, so the definition means 'displaying toadyism'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone showing toadyism is fawning and servile, which is what sycophantish describes.

clue.text: Spot anonymous test-driver by dam?

parts.note: The Stig is the masked, nameless test driver on TV's Top Gear
a dam is an animal's mother

explanation.surface: Catch sight of the faceless test driver next to a reservoir wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dam' suggests a water barrier; here it is a mother. The Stig is the helmeted test driver of the BBC car show Top Gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A stigma is a mark or blemish on the skin, so it is a spot.

clue.text: Meddler, coach starts to bring on decline in two years

parts.note: a coach is a long-distance bus

indicators.note: placed in the pair, so it sits between them

parts.note: Y is the abbreviation for year, twice

indicators.note: the starts of words are their first letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A nosy parker blames a coach company for two years of decline.
explanation.definitionFit: A busybody is an interfering person who pokes into others' affairs, a meddler.

clue.text: Ostentatious point, mostly nonsense, is ultimately rubbish

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a peak is a pointed mountain top
informal for rubbish talk, as in cock and bull
taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately points at the last letter, the only one kept

parts.note: final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A showy argument, mostly nonsense, is in the end rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: A peacock flaunts its tail, so peacockish describes showy, vain behaviour, which is ostentatious.

clue.text: These thrust to and fro in big ships when holding inlet control off and on

indicators.note: the ships holding something carry it inside them

parts.note: ocean liners
an arm of the sea is an inlet

indicators.note: skipping one and taking the next keeps every second letter only

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Machinery that drives big ships back and forth when they hold an inlet in check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off and on' starts with off, so the even letters are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: A linear motor produces straight-line thrust rather than rotation, so it pushes a load forwards and backwards.

clue.text: We rapidly brush moustache

definitions.meaning: first meaning: people who whisk, sweeping quickly
second meaning: the hair growing on a man's face

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a whimsical agent noun: those who whisk are whisk-ers, and 'we' could say we do it.
explanation.definitionFit: Facial hair on the upper lip and cheeks is called whiskers, and a moustache is that growth.

clue.text: Fake setter's set on job, filling in form

parts.note: the setter says I'm, contracting I am
a post is a job or position

indicators.note: the filling of a word is its inside, so the outer letters are dropped

parts.note: the inner letters of the word

explanation.surface: A crossword setter, keen on getting a job, fills in an application form under false pretences.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'set on' means placed above, so the setter's part sits over the job.
explanation.definitionFit: An impostor is someone who pretends to be another, a fraud, so the noun fake fits.

clue.text: Furnishings on coach drive clergy close to nuts

parts.note: to hammer in a nail is to drive it
the cloth is a collective term for the clergy

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so its final letter is kept

parts.note: final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Fitments on a coach drive the clergy close to madness.
explanation.definitionFit: A hammercloth is the ornamental cloth covering the driver's seat of a horse-drawn coach, a piece of its furnishings.

clue.text: Dramatist's brief obstacle

indicators.note: made brief means cut short, so the last letter is removed

parts.note: a barrier is an obstacle

explanation.surface: A playwright's short hurdle.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: J M Barrie was the Scottish playwright who wrote Peter Pan, so he is a dramatist.

clue.text: Imp, back to front, shows wit

indicators.note: a letter taken from the back goes to the front, moving round in order

parts.note: a sprite is an elf or imp

explanation.surface: A mischievous imp turned around reveals some cleverness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back to front' tempts a full reversal, but only the final letter moves to the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Esprit is French-derived for lively intelligence and quick humour, which is wit.

clue.text: This would keep Oxford perhaps on 6

definitions.text: This would keep Oxford perhaps on 6

parts.words: This would keep Oxford perhaps on 6
parts.note: surface reading: something that holds a university city in place
setter's reading: an Oxford is a lace-up shoe, and 6 Across is the body part it is worn on

explanation.walkthrough: Oxford reads as the city, but it is a style of lace-up shoe; entry 6 supplies the extremity it stays on.
explanation.definitionFit: A lace threaded through a shoe's eyelets holds the shoe secure on the wearer's foot.

clue.text: Maybe Nigella's deleting university's historical records

indicators.note: deleting means striking something out, so one letter is removed

parts.note: nigella, love-in-a-mist, is an example of a plant that flowers for one year
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Perhaps the TV cook Nigella is dropping her university's chronicles.
explanation.walkthrough: Nigella suggests the cook Nigella Lawson; here nigellas are the garden flowers, examples of annuals.
explanation.definitionFit: Annals are year-by-year chronicles of events, the historical records of a body or nation.

clue.text: Medium for culture absorbed by first cosmonaut?

indicators.note: something absorbed by a name lies inside it, so the letters around it are stripped away

explanation.walkthrough: The containing name is not printed: think of Yuri Gagarin, then drop his surname's first letter and last two to leave the answer sitting inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Agar is the jelly from seaweed used in laboratories as a growth medium for bacterial cultures.

clue.text: Warms up unopened food

indicators.note: left unopened means without its opening, so the first letter goes

parts.note: heats means warms up

explanation.definitionFit: Eats is informal for food, as in 'good eats'.

clue.text: On reflection, one may watch a trailer in this

definitions.text: On reflection, one may watch a trailer in this

parts.words: On reflection, one may watch a trailer in this
parts.note: surface reading: after some thought, a place to see a film preview, such as a cinema
setter's reading: a driver checks a towed caravan by its image in a mirror on the side of the car

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trailer' suggests a film preview and 'on reflection' means after thought; both are literal here, a towed vehicle seen as a reflected image.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's side-mounted mirror lets the driver keep an eye on a towed caravan or trailer behind.

clue.text: Nimble agent checks resistance

indicators.note: to check something is to hold it back, so the agent holds the letter within

parts.note: a secret agent
the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: An agile secret agent keeps the resistance under control.
explanation.definitionFit: Spry describes someone, usually older, who is still lively and quick on their feet, so agile.

clue.text: Choir in Utrecht performing astride cross and font

indicators.note: one thing placed in another goes inside it
sitting astride something straddles it, with legs either side
performers move about, so the letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: abbreviation for choir
taken as written
the letter shaped like a cross

explanation.surface: A choir singing in Utrecht stands over a cross and a baptismal font.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Font' reads as the church basin for baptism, but it is a typeface. The choir's abbreviation joins the city's letters before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Church Text is the name of a black-letter typeface, so it is a font in the printing sense.
